claim: Human LBR is essential for cholesterol synthesis.
source: We demonstrate that human LBR is essential for cholesterol synthesis.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including knockout cell lines, cholesterol starvation assays, and metabolic labeling.

claim: LBR mutant derivatives implicated in Greenberg skeletal dysplasia or Pelger-Huët anomaly fail to rescue the cholesterol auxotrophy of a LBR-deficient human cell line.
source: LBR mutant derivatives implicated in Greenberg skeletal dysplasia or Pelger-Huët anomaly fail to rescue the cholesterol auxotrophy of a LBR-deficient human cell line, consistent with a loss-of-function mechanism for these congenital disorders.
evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiments in LBR knockout cells with disease-associated mutations (Figure 4).

claim: Disease-causing LBR variants fall into two classes: point mutations in the sterol reductase domain that perturb enzymatic activity by reducing the affinity for NADPH, and LBR truncations that render the mutant protein metabolically unstable.
source: These disease-causing variants fall into two classes: point mutations in the sterol reductase domain perturb enzymatic activity by reducing the affinity for the essential cofactor NADPH, while LBR truncations render the mutant protein metabolically unstable, leading to its rapid degradation at the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: Supported by NADPH binding assays (Figure 5D) and pulse-chase experiments (Figure 6).

claim: Point mutations in the sterol reductase domain reduce the affinity for the essential cofactor NADPH.
source: point mutations in the sterol reductase domain perturb enzymatic activity by reducing the affinity for the essential cofactor NADPH
evidence: Demonstrated by NADPH binding assays showing reduced affinity for N547D and R583Q mutants (Figure 5D).

claim: LBR truncations lead to rapid degradation of the mutant protein at the inner nuclear membrane.
source: LBR truncations render the mutant protein metabolically unstable, leading to its rapid degradation at the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: Shown by pulse-chase experiments demonstrating rapid degradation of LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* (Figure 6).

claim: Metabolically unstable LBR variants may serve as model substrates for investigating protein turnover mechanisms at the inner nuclear membrane of higher eukaryotes.
source: Thus, metabolically unstable LBR variants may serve as long-sought-after model substrates enabling previously impossible investigations of poorly understood protein turnover mechanisms at the inner nuclear membrane of higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a prospective claim based on the observed properties of the mutants.

claim: LBR is an evolutionary conserved, multifunctional protein.
source: Lamin B receptor (LBR) is an evolutionary conserved, multifunctional protein (Olins et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The N-terminal moiety of LBR resides in the nucleoplasm and contains a chromatin-binding TUDOR domain.
source: The N-terminal moiety of LBR, which resides in the nucleoplasm, contains a chromatin-binding TUDOR domain and associates with the nuclear lamina (Makatsori et al., 2004; Pyrpasopoulou et al., 1996; Worman et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The N-terminal moiety of LBR associates with the nuclear lamina.
source: The N-terminal moiety of LBR, which resides in the nucleoplasm, contains a chromatin-binding TUDOR domain and associates with the nuclear lamina (Makatsori et al., 2004; Pyrpasopoulou et al., 1996; Worman et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The polytopic C-terminal domain anchors LBR in the inner nuclear membrane.
source: while the polytopic C-terminal domain anchors LBR in the inner nuclear membrane (INM) and has sequence homology to sterol C14 reductases (Li et al., 2015; Silve et al., 1998; Worman et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The C-terminal domain of LBR has sequence homology to sterol C14 reductases.
source: while the polytopic C-terminal domain anchors LBR in the inner nuclear membrane (INM) and has sequence homology to sterol C14 reductases (Li et al., 2015; Silve et al., 1998; Worman et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sterol C14 reductases are widely conserved throughout evolution.
source: Sterol C14 reductases are widely conserved throughout evolution and are responsible for the reduction of a specific carbon-carbon double bond as part of the tightly controlled enzymatic cascade which results in the production of cholesterol and cholesterol-related compounds (Benveniste, 2004; Holmer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sterol C14 reductases are responsible for the reduction of a specific carbon-carbon double bond in cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: Sterol C14 reductases are widely conserved throughout evolution and are responsible for the reduction of a specific carbon-carbon double bond as part of the tightly controlled enzymatic cascade which results in the production of cholesterol and cholesterol-related compounds (Benveniste, 2004; Holmer et al., 1998) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is currently no known functional connection between the chromatin-binding N-terminus of LBR and the sterol reductase C-terminus of the protein.
source: There is currently no known functional connection between the chromatin-binding N-terminus of LBR and the sterol reductase C-terminus of the protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Human cells have a second C14 sterol reductase enzyme called TM7SF2.
source: The function of the sterol reductase domain (SRD) of LBR is further obfuscated by the fact that human cells have a second C14 sterol reductase enzyme called TM7SF2, which is conserved in evolution and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where other enzymes responsible for cholesterol biogenesis are typically found (Bennati et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TM7SF2 is conserved in evolution and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: The function of the sterol reductase domain (SRD) of LBR is further obfuscated by the fact that human cells have a second C14 sterol reductase enzyme called TM7SF2, which is conserved in evolution and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where other enzymes responsible for cholesterol biogenesis are typically found (Bennati et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The TM7SF2 promoter harbors a sterol response element (SRE).
source: The TM7SF2 promoter harbors a sterol response element (SRE) common to most, if not all enzymes implicated in cholesterol synthesis, allowing for the tight regulation of their transcription in response to cholesterol availability (Brown and Goldstein, 1999; Sharpe and Brown, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The LBR gene lacks an SRE consensus sequence and is constitutively expressed.
source: However, the LBR gene lacks an SRE consensus sequence and is constitutively expressed (Bennati et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2008; Sharpe and Brown, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two congenital disorders are known to be associated with mutations in LBR: Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia.
source: Two congenital disorders are known to be associated with mutations in LBR: Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia (Oosterwijk et al., 2003; Shultz et al., 2003; Wassif et al., 2007; Waterham et al., 2003) (see Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and Table 1.

claim: Pelger-Huët anomaly is an autosomal dominant disorder in which a single mutation in one LBR allele results in abnormal hypolobulation of granulocyte nuclei.
source: Pelger-Huët anomaly is an autosomal dominant disorder in which a single mutation in one LBR allele results in abnormal hypolobulation of granulocyte nuclei (Best et al., 2003; Hoffmann et al., 2002; Shultz et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Greenberg skeletal dysplasia is a perinatally lethal, autosomal recessive condition that results in abnormal bone development, fetal hydrops, and the ultimate nonviability of the fetus.
source: Greenberg skeletal dysplasia, is a perinatally lethal, autosomal recessive condition that results in abnormal bone development, fetal hydrops, and the ultimate nonviability of the fetus (Chitayat et al., 1993; Greenberg et al., 1988; Horn et al., 2000; Konstantinidou et al., 2008; Trajkovski et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Greenberg skeletal dysplasia results from the inheritance of two mutant LBR alleles that when heterozygous cause Pelger-Huët anomaly.
source: Interestingly, mounting evidence indicates that Greenberg skeletal dysplasia results from the inheritance of two mutant LBR alleles that when heterozygous cause Pelger-Huët anomaly (Konstantinidou et al., 2008; Oosterwijk et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The two diseases (Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia) represent different allelic states of the same chromosomal lesion.
source: indicating that the two diseases represent different allelic states of the same chromosomal lesion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence about the genetic relationship between the two diseases.

claim: It is unclear whether Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia are caused by structural changes in the nuclear lamina, or whether they are diseases of cholesterol metabolism.
source: However, it is unclear whether these diseases are caused by structural changes in the nuclear lamina, or whether they are diseases of cholesterol metabolism (Clayton et al., 2010; Olins et al., 2010; Wassif et al., 2007; Waterham et al., 2003; Worman and Bonne, 2007).
evidence: This statement reflects uncertainty in the field prior to this study, supported by citations.

claim: LBR knockout HeLa cells were generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system.
source: In order to clarify the cellular function of LBR both in cholesterol metabolism and as a structural component of the nuclear lamina, we used the CRISPR/Cas9 system (Mali et al., 2013) to generate LBR knockout HeLa cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation and reference to supplementary figure.

claim: A clone was obtained that yielded no detectable LBR protein as judged by immunoblotting.
source: A clone was obtained that yielded no detectable LBR protein as judged by immunoblotting, corresponding to the absence of a PCR product of the size predicted by the wild-type LBR allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that all LBR alleles had been effectively targeted.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HeLa cells are aneuploid, including three complete copies of chromosome 1 where the LBR gene is located.
source: Since HeLa cells are aneuploid, including three complete copies of chromosome 1 where the LBR gene is located, any LBR knockout should have three distinct genome 'edits'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HeLa cells.

claim: Sequence analysis revealed three distinct mutant alleles, all containing frame-shift mutations or premature stop codons within the 5' region of the LBR open reading frame.
source: Indeed, sequence analysis revealed three distinct mutant alleles, all containing frame-shift mutations or premature stop codons within the 5' region of the LBR open reading frame, showing that no more than 12 amino acids of LBR WT sequence can be produced from any of the three mutant alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences in overall cell morphology or growth were observed between WT and LBR KO cells under normal growth conditions.
source: No differences in overall cell morphology or growth were observed between WT and LBR KO cells under normal growth conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No change in the localization of Lamin B1, Lamin A/C or Emerin was found in LBR KO cells compared to control cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found no change in the localization of Lamin B1, Lamin A/C or Emerin in LBR KO cells compared to control cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of LBR had no effect on the localization of Sun1 or Sun2.
source: Similarly, we found that the absence of LBR also had no effect on the localization of other structural proteins of the NE such as Sun1 or Sun2, which serve as the INM components of the LINC (linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton) complex (Crisp et al., 2006) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: In both WT and LBR KO cells, the inner and outer nuclear membranes were regularly spaced and featured a nuclear lamina and nuclear pores of normal morphology.
source: We found that in both WT and LBR KO cells, the inner and outer nuclear membranes were regularly spaced and featured a nuclear lamina and nuclear pores of normal morphology (Figure 2B, arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LBR does not play a significant role in maintaining NE integrity in HeLa cells.
source: These data, together with our previous observations by immunofluorescence microscopy, indicate that in these cells, LBR does not play a significant role in maintaining NE integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron microscopy and immunofluorescence data.

claim: After 4 days under cholesterol-restrictive growth conditions LBR KO, but not WT HeLa cells exhibited slow growth, cell rounding, and detachment, followed quickly by cell death on days 5–7.
source: We found that after 4 days under cholesterol-restrictive growth conditions LBR KO, but not WT HeLa cells exhibited slow growth, cell rounding, and detachment, followed quickly by cell death on days 5–7 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bright-field microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Addition of 10 µM exogenous cholesterol to the cell culture medium effectively rescued the observed sensitivity of LBR KO cells to low-cholesterol growth conditions.
source: Addition of 10 µM exogenous cholesterol to the cell culture medium effectively rescued the observed sensitivity of LBR KO cells to low-cholesterol growth conditions (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by bright-field microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed growth defect of LBR KO cells was rescued by the addition of low density lipoprotein (LDL) particles to the cell culture medium.
source: The observed growth defect of LBR KO cells was also rescued by the addition of low density lipoprotein (LDL) particles, a physiologically relevant cholesterol carrier (Lodish, 2013), to the cell culture medium (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by bright-field microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and citation.

claim: The primary function of LBR in the tissue culture model is to sustain cholesterol biogenesis when the extracellular supply of cholesterol is scarce.
source: These results suggest that the primary function of LBR in our tissue culture model is to sustain cholesterol biogenesis when the extracellular supply of cholesterol is scarce.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with cholesterol and LDL.

claim: Newly synthesized cholesterol was readily detected in WT cells but there was a near-complete loss of cholesterol synthesis in LBR KO cells.
source: We readily detected newly synthesized cholesterol in WT cells, as judged by its co-migration with purified 14C cholesterol, which was included as a standard (Figure 2D). Notably, we observed a near-complete loss of cholesterol synthesis in LBR KO cells (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by metabolic labeling and TLC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A strong reduction of viability was observed in LBR-silenced HFF cells under cholesterol-restrictive conditions.
source: In either case, we observed a strong reduction of viability in LBR-silenced cells under cholesterol-restrictive conditions, whereas control cells transfected with non-targeting siRNAs displayed normal cell morphology under these conditions (Figure 3 A,B,D,E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and viability assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A strong reduction of viability was observed in LBR-silenced HEK293T cells under cholesterol-restrictive conditions.
source: In either case, we observed a strong reduction of viability in LBR-silenced cells under cholesterol-restrictive conditions, whereas control cells transfected with non-targeting siRNAs displayed normal cell morphology under these conditions (Figure 3 A,B,D,E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy and viability assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HFF and HeLa cells upregulated TM7SF2 under starvation conditions.
source: As expected (Bennati et al., 2006), we found that HFF and HeLa cells upregulated TM7SF2 under starvation conditions (Figure 3G)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G and citation.

claim: LBR was constitutively expressed and unresponsive to cholesterol starvation.
source: whereas LBR was constitutively expressed and unresponsive to cholesterol starvation (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: HEK293T cells did not materially up-regulate TM7SF2 on the transcript level.
source: Interestingly, HEK293T cells did not materially up-regulate TM7SF2 on the transcript level (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The abundance of the TM7SF2 protein in HFF and HeLa cells increased under cholesterol-restrictive conditions.
source: The abundance of the TM7SF2 protein in HFF and HeLa cells increased under cholesterol-restrictive conditions, whereas HEK293T cells displayed somewhat higher levels of TM7SF2 even under normal conditions but did not upregulate TM7SF2 to the same degree as HFF or HeLa cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: No significant differences were observed between HeLa WT and HeLa LBR KO cells in their ability to up-regulate TM7SF2 on the transcript level.
source: We did not observe significant differences between HeLa WT and HeLa LBR KO cells in their ability to up-regulate TM7SF2 on the transcript level, as judged by qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The observed upregulation of TM7SF2 was dependent on SREBP2.
source: In accordance with previous findings (Bennati et al., 2006), the observed upregulation was dependent on SREBP2, as judged by a profound reduction of TM7SF2 and HMG-CoA reductase on the transcript levels in cells depleted of SREBP2 via RNA interference.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data after SREBP2 knockdown and citation.

claim: The isolated TM7SF2 cDNA contains the entire coding sequence of the published transcript variant 1 (NM_003273), with no apparent mutations.
source: This isolated cDNA (1401 bp) contains the entire coding sequence (CDS) of the published transcript variant 1 (NM_003273), with no apparent mutations as evidenced by a sequence alignment to the CDS of NM_003273 (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data.

claim: LBR is essential for cholesterol synthesis in several human cell lines despite the presence of TM7SF2.
source: Based on the foregoing, we arrive at the conclusion that LBR is essential for cholesterol synthesis in several human cell lines despite the presence of TM7SF2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from multiple cell lines showing LBR essentiality despite TM7SF2 expression.

claim: Expression of LBR WT from the FlpIn locus completely rescued the growth defect observed for LBR KO cells in cholesterol starvation growth medium.
source: We found that expression of LBR WT from the FlpIn locus completely rescued the growth defect observed for LBR KO cells in cholesterol starvation growth medium (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by cell growth and imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: All four disease-associated LBR alleles failed to rescue the observed growth defect.
source: Importantly, all four disease-associated LBR alleles failed to rescue the observed growth defect (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by cell growth and imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: LBR KO cells were found to have approximately 40% less total cholesterol content than LBR WT cells after 7 days of cholesterol starvation.
source: LBR KO cells were found to have approximately 40% less total cholesterol content than LBR WT cells after 7 days of cholesterol starvation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by cholesterol quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cellular cholesterol content was fully restored to that of WT cells by expression of LBR WT from the FlpIn locus.
source: Cellular cholesterol content was fully restored to that of WT cells by expression of LBR WT from the FlpIn locus even at somewhat lower LBR expression levels compared to WT cells (Figure 4D and E)
evidence: Supported by cholesterol quantification and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Neither cell growth nor cellular cholesterol content are restored by the expression of LBR N547D, LBR R583Q, LBR 1402TΔ or LBR 1600* in a LBR KO background.
source: Neither cell growth nor cellular cholesterol content are restored by the expression of LBR N547D, LBR R583Q, LBR 1402TΔ or LBR 1600* in a LBR KO background, indicating that these genetic lesions ultimately result in a failure to sustain cell growth under cholesterol-restrictive conditions.
evidence: Supported by cell growth and cholesterol quantification data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both the isolated LBR SRD and the fusion protein SUN2-LBR rescued the LBR KO phenotype.
source: Finally, both the isolated LBR SRD and the fusion protein SUN2-LBR rescued the LBR KO phenotype.
evidence: Supported by cell growth data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SRD is necessary and sufficient for survival of cholesterol-starved cells.
source: Given that all constructs were expressed at levels higher than the rescuing WT allele (Figure 5B), our results indicate that the SRD is necessary and sufficient for survival of cholesterol-starved cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with domain constructs shown in Figure 5.

claim: LBR N547 and R583 residues correspond to maSR1 N359 and R395, respectively, both of which map to the NADPH binding pocket.
source: Based on a sequence alignment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the LBR N547 and R583 residues correspond to maSR1 N359 and R395, respectively, both of which map to the NADPH binding pocket, with N359 being implicated in a hydrogen bond formation with a phosphate oxygen of NADPH (Li et al., 2015) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment and structural data from the cited crystal structure.

claim: WT LBR displayed hyperbolic saturation for NADPH with a KD of 24.2 µM.
source: WT LBR displayed hyperbolic saturation for the cofactor with a KD of 24.2 µM.
evidence: Supported by NADPH binding assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both LBR N547D and LBR R583Q mutants had a severely decreased binding affinity to NADPH, with N547D having the strongest effect.
source: Both mutants had a severely decreased binding affinity to NADPH, with N547D having the strongest effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by NADPH binding assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Neither LBR N547D nor LBR 583Q transgenes efficiently restored de novo cholesterol synthesis in LBR KO cells.
source: As expected, neither LBR N547D nor LBR 583Q transgenes efficiently restored de novo cholesterol synthesis in LBR KO cells, which was monitored by metabolic incorporation of 14C acetate into cholesterol (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by metabolic labeling and TLC data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Neither of the LBR C-terminal truncation mutant proteins (1402TΔ or 1600*) were detected via immunoblotting using an LBR antibody that recognizes the N-terminal domain of LBR.
source: Neither of the LBR C-terminal truncation mutant proteins (1402TΔ or 1600*) were detected via immunoblotting using an LBR antibody that recognizes the N-terminal (nuclear) domain of LBR (see Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LBR WT, LBR N547D and LBR R583Q are extremely stable.
source: We found that LBR WT, LBR N547D and LBR R583Q are extremely stable (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The lack of cofactor binding does not lead to LBR instability.
source: indicating that the lack of cofactor binding does not lead to LBR instability.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stability of N547D and R583Q mutants despite their reduced NADPH binding.

claim: Both truncated LBR variants (1402TΔ and 1600*) were produced at levels comparable to WT LBR at the beginning of the chase period but were rapidly degraded.
source: In contrast, both truncated LBR variants were produced at levels comparable to WT LBR at the beginning of the chase period but were rapidly degraded (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Both LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* proteins were degraded extremely rapidly, with little or no protein remaining after 30 min.
source: We found that both LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* proteins were degraded extremely rapidly, with little or no protein remaining after 30 min (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Both LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* mutants were significantly stabilized by MG132.
source: Both mutants were significantly stabilized by MG132, with minimal degradation taking place in 60 min after synthesis.
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data with MG132 treatment shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The degradation of truncated LBR variants depends on the proteasome.
source: We conclude that the degradation of truncated LBR variants depends on the proteasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stabilization of mutants by the proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: The kinetics of LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* degradation were remarkably rapid, with half-lives of 10–15 min.
source: Notably, the kinetics of LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* degradation were remarkably rapid, with half-lives of 10–15 min
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 6.

claim: HA-Ub conjugated species were significantly more abundant for both LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* than for LBR WT in both untreated and MG132-treated samples.
source: As expected, HA-Ub conjugated species were significantly more abundant for both LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* than for LBR WT in both untreated and MG132-treated samples, with the latter condition leading to an additional increase (Figure 7B, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The metabolic instability of LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* is caused by degradation via the Ub/proteasome system (UPS).
source: Together, the data argue that the metabolic instability of LBR 1402TΔ and LBR 1600* is caused by degradation via the Ub/proteasome system (UPS).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ubiquitylation and proteasome-dependence data.

claim: In the absence of MG132, LBR 1402TΔ is partitioned between the ER and the NE.
source: In the absence of MG132, LBR 1402TΔ is partitioned between the ER and the NE, as judged by a co-staining with anti-LBR and anti-Lamin A/C antibodies (Figure 8A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LBR 1600* displays nuclear rim staining that is indistinguishable from LBR WT.
source: LBR 1600*, on the other hand, displays nuclear rim staining that is indistinguishable from LBR WT (Figure 8B, left panel; cf. Figure 2A, upper left panel) (Worman et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8B and citation.

claim: Both truncated LBR proteins appear to accumulate in the nucleoplasm upon proteasomal inhibition.
source: Against all expectations, both truncated LBR proteins appear to accumulate in the nucleoplasm upon proteasomal inhibition (Figure 8A and B, right panels).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Both LBR mutants are clearly excluded from nucleoli in the presence of MG132.
source: In addition, both LBR mutants are clearly excluded from nucleoli in the presence of MG132.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: MG132 treatment resulted in a shift from a non-nuclear to a nuclear LBR immunofluorescence signal for both mutants.
source: We observe that with both mutants, MG132 treatment resulted in a shift from a non-nuclear to a nuclear LBR immunofluorescence signal, with LBR 1402TΔ showing a slightly larger shift in localization than LBR 1600*, which resides primarily in the nuclear compartment even in the absence of MG132 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Disease-associated, C-terminally truncated LBR mutants accumulate in the nuclear compartment, rather than the ER or cytosol, after MG132 treatment.
source: These unexpected results indicate that disease-associated, C-terminally truncated LBR mutants surprisingly accumulate in the nuclear compartment, rather than the ER or cytosol, after MG132 treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy data showing nuclear accumulation.

claim: p97 WT had no effect on LBR 1600* degradation.
source: As expected, p97 WT had no effect on LBR 1600* degradation (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: p97 QQ inhibited LBR 1600* turnover to an extent that is comparable to proteasomal inhibition.
source: However, p97 QQ inhibited LBR 1600* turnover to an extent that is comparable to proteasomal inhibition (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: In the presence of both p97 WT and MG132, LBR 1600* accumulates in the nucleoplasm and to a lesser degree, the ER.
source: In the presence of both p97 WT and MG132, we observed the expected LBR 1600* accumulation in the nucleoplasm and to a lesser degree, the ER (Figure 8F)
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: LBR 1600* accumulates nearly quantitatively at the nuclear rim in the presence of p97 QQ even in the presence of MG132.
source: whereas LBR 1600* accumulates nearly quantitatively at the nuclear rim in the presence of p97 QQ even in the presence of MG132.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The data are consistent with a blockage of the membrane dislocation step at the INM by p97 QQ.
source: The data are consistent with a blockage of the membrane dislocation step at the INM (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy data showing nuclear rim accumulation with p97 QQ.

claim: Only a small percentage of LBR 1600* is degraded by the canonical ERAD pathway.
source: In conclusion, these results are consistent with a mechanism in which only a small percentage of LBR 1600* is degraded by the canonical ERAD pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization and degradation data.

claim: The majority of LBR 1600* is localized to the INM, where a second quality control pathway operates to extract and destroy it in a series of reactions employing both p97 and the UPS.
source: The majority of the truncated protein is localized to the INM, where it appears that a second quality control pathway operates to extract and destroy LBR 1600* in a series of reactions employing both p97 and the UPS (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization, p97-dependence, and proteasome-dependence data.

claim: Previous studies in mice reported that the sterol reductase activities of LBR and TM7SF2 are functionally redundant.
source: These results are unexpected since previous studies in mice reported that the sterol reductase activities of LBR and TM7SF2 are functionally redundant, suggesting that HEM dysplasia is likely a laminopathy that is unrelated to the sterol reductase activity of LBR (Wassif et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: In cultured HeLa cells, LBR does not play a significant role in NE organization despite being a constitutively expressed, abundant INM component.
source: In cultured HeLa cells, however, LBR does not play a significant role in NE organization despite being a constitutively expressed, abundant INM component (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microscopy data showing no changes in NE structure in LBR KO cells.

claim: Mice lacking a fully functional LBR allele due to homozygous mutations at the ichthyosis locus (ic/ic) are viable, although these animals display numerous phenotypic abnormalities.
source: Nevertheless, it is striking that mice lacking a fully functional LBR allele due to homozygous mutations at the ichthyosis locus (ic/ic) are viable, although these animals display numerous phenotypic abnormalities including alopecia, syndactyly and hydrocephalus as well as an increase in embryonic lethality (Shultz et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in mouse models.

claim: Growth defects were observed in primary cells isolated from mouse models with mutations in the LBR gene.
source: Growth defects were also observed in primary cells isolated from mouse models with mutations in the LBR gene (Subramanian et al., 2012; Verhagen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in mouse models.

claim: Defects in neutrophil maturation in ic/ic animals can be rescued in vitro by expression of the LBR SRD.
source: Of note, defects in neutrophil maturation in ic/ic animals can be recued in vitro by expression of the LBR SRD (Subramanian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in mouse models.

claim: LBR function is subject to diversification in the course of evolution.
source: It is likely that LBR function is subject to diversification in the course of evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on comparative observations across species.

claim: Human LBR can rescue sterol reductase deficiency in yeast.

source: while LBR from Droshophila melanogaster does not complement this phenotype (Wagner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is a cholesterol-auxotrophic organism.
source: Since D. melanogaster is a cholesterol-auxotrophic organism

claim: The Tudor domain of LBR is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis.
source: While we found this domain to be dispensable for cholesterol synthesis (Figure 5A)

claim: The LBR SRD is necessary and sufficient to restore cholesterol synthesis and rescues a defect in neutrophil maturation observed in ic/ic cells in vitro.
source: Since the LBR SRD is neccesary and sufficient to restore cholesterol synthesis (Figure 5A) and rescues a defect in neutrophil maturation observed in ic/ic cells in vitro (Subramanian et al., 2012)

claim: Cholesterol synthesis can proceed through differential, tissue-specific usage of distinct yet interchangeable segments of the established synthesis pathways.
source: Since cholesterol synthesis can proceed through differential, tissue-specific usage of distinct yet interchangeable segments of the established synthesis pathways (Mitsche et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings.

claim: TM7SF2 may participate in healing of burn wounds.
source: Interestingly, a recent study suggested that TM7SF2 may participate in healing of burn wounds (Lei et al., 2016), possibly representing a case of a more specialized physiological role.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings.

claim: All tested disease-causing mutations in LBR fail to complement the cholesterol auxotrophy imposed by an LBR deficiency in the tissue culture model.
source: Based on our finding that all tested disease-causing mutations in LBR fail to complement the cholesterol auxotrophy imposed by an LBR deficiency in our tissue culture model (Figure 4)
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: C-terminally truncated LBR proteins found in both Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia are rapidly degraded by a proteasome-dependent protein quality-control pathway that appears to be distinct from the canonical ERAD pathway.
source: Another unexpected outcome of this study is that C-terminally truncated LBR proteins found in both Pelger-Huët anomaly and Greenberg skeletal dysplasia are rapidly degraded by a proteasome-dependent protein quality-control pathway that appears to be distinct from the canonical ERAD pathway (Figures 8, 9).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase, ubiquitylation, and microscopy data shown in Figures 6-8.

claim: INM-resident proteins are synthesized in the ER prior to their targeting to the INM.
source: Given that INM-resident proteins are synthesized in the ER prior to their targeting to the INM (Lusk et al., 2007; Ungricht and Kutay, 2015)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The correctly folded N-terminal moiety of LBR containing INM targeting information leads to the rapid trafficking of LBR 1600* to the INM before elements of the ERAD pathway can act.
source: we propose that the correctly folded N-terminal moiety of LBR containing INM targeting information (Smith and Blobel, 1993; Soullam and Worman, 1993) leads to the rapid trafficking of LBR 1600* to the INM before elements of the ERAD pathway can act (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the localization data and citations to previous work on INM targeting.

claim: Near-quantitative nuclear accumulation of an HA-tagged LBR variant is achieved in ~20 min.
source: Considering that near-quantitative nuclear accumulation of an HA-tagged LBR variant is achieved in ~20 min (Ungricht et al., 2015)

claim: The half life of LBR 1600* is ~10–15 min.
source: and that the half life of LBR 1600* is ~10–15 min

claim: A significant fraction of LBR 1600* escapes the ERAD system leading to localization to the INM mediated by the intact N-terminal domain.

Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrating INM localization of LBR 1600* under steady-state conditions).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetics and localization data.

claim: Upon arrival of LBR 1600* at the INM, a system analogous to but distinct from the known ERAD system is responsible for the ubiquitylation of LBR 1600* and its p97-dependent extraction from the INM.
source: Upon arrival of LBR 1600* at the INM, a system analogous to but distinct from the known ERAD system is responsible for the ubiquitylation of LBR 1600* and its p97-dependent extraction from the INM (Figures 8, 9).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the ubiquitylation, p97-dependence, and localization data.

claim: The INM degradative system is different from the established ERAD machinery.
source: Based on the unusually rapid kinetics and substantial protein accumulation in a dislocated nuclear state in presence of MG132, we believe that the INM degradative system is different from the established ERAD machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetics and localization data.

claim: It is still unclear which Ub ligases account for protein turnover at the INM of mammalian cells.
source: In fact, it is still unclear which Ub ligases account for protein turnover at the INM of mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanisms of protein quality control operative at the NE of budding yeast are far better understood than analogous systems in mammalian cells.
source: In general, the mechanisms of protein quality control operative at the NE of budding yeast are far better understood than analogous systems in mammalian cells (Deng and Hochstrasser, 2006; Foresti et al., 2014; Khmelinskii et al., 2014; Rose and Schlieker, 2012; Webster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The absence of suitable model substrates has been the major limitation for studying protein quality control at the NE in higher eukaryotes.
source: The absence of suitable model substrates in higher eukaryotes has been the major limitation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: This study establishes the methodological framework to investigate NE-directed quality control mechanisms in human cells.
source: This study establishes the long sought-after methodological framework to investigate NE-directed quality control mechanisms in human cells.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the study.

claim: The combination of the extremely short half-life of LBR1600*, its near-exclusive localization to the INM, and ease with which LBR1600* can be arrested at distinct stages of dislocation and turnover make this LBR variant an ideal tool to pursue mechanistic studies.
source: We propose that the combination of (i) the extremely short half-life of LBR1600*, (ii) its near-exclusive localization to the INM as well as (iii) and ease with which LBR1600* can be arrested at distinct stages of dislocation and turnover make this LBR variant an ideal tool to pursue mechanistic studies aimed at the elucidation of protein quality control and turnover at the INM.
evidence: This is a prospective claim about the utility of the findings.

claim: Both Bloch and Kandutsch-Russel pathways employ an NADPH-dependent reduction step which can be catalyzed by sterol C14 reductases LBR or TM7SF2.
